400.title: The path, closed
400.hook: eight factors, walked together, not one after another
400.howItsDone: Buddhists across schools teach the eight factors as three trainings, virtue, concentration and wisdom, developed together rather than in sequence; the eight-spoked wheel is widely used as a symbol of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth jhana, where even pleasure is set down. Your line: wrapped in white.

A wheel doesn't turn one spoke at a time. Forty-eight days ago, this stretch opened with a wheel of eight spokes, and the nun Dhammadinna sorting them into three trainings. Since then the spokes have come out one by one: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. That's how you learn a list. But the suttas don't describe walking the path that way. Today the spokes go back in.
screen: `ONE WHEEL, EIGHT SPOKES.` → `LEARNED ONE AT A TIME.` → `TODAY THEY GO BACK IN.`

segments.voice: Here they are once more: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Dhammadinna showed how they sort into virtue, concentration and wisdom. The Great Forty, MN 117, shows how they feed each other. In one who has right view, the Buddha says, right intention comes into being. From right intention, right speech; from right speech, right action; from right action, right livelihood; and on down the line, each factor giving rise to the next, as far as right concentration. Then the sutta keeps going: from right concentration, right knowledge, and from right knowledge, right liberation. Eight factors for one in training; ten for one who has arrived. The same sutta has view, effort and mindfulness running around each of the others, so the chain isn't a ladder you climb once. Nobody finishes right view before starting right speech. You speak a little more carefully, and your view clears a little. Your view clears, and your work changes. Your work changes, and the mind gathers more easily. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's translation: “The best of ways is the eightfold.” The Pali word for path, magga, is the ordinary word for a road. And nobody walks a road with all the left steps first. Both feet, the whole way.
screen: `VIRTUE, CONCENTRATION, WISDOM.` · `EACH FACTOR GIVES RISE TO THE NEXT.` · `TEN FOR THE ONE WHO HAS ARRIVED.` · `BOTH FEET, THE WHOLE WAY.` · then, large: `EIGHT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Let the eight pass through, one breath each: view, seeing things as they are; intention, goodwill; speech, today's words; action, harming no one; livelihood, your work; effort, the good you keep going; mindfulness, this breath; concentration, gathered here. Then let go of the list, and sit with all eight at once, nothing left out.
The path. Eight factors, walked together like the spokes of one wheel, each one strengthening the rest.
Your line: eight together. Each one, walked, makes the others easier. Four hundred days; see you tomorrow.

401.title: The Middle-Length Sayings
401.hook: 152 discourses of middle length; we read highlights in order, with Chalmers' translation
401.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Majjhima Nikaya is studied in monasteries and recited in Pali, and many lay Buddhists read it in translation; its suttas are often the texts teachers return to for instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the path, eight factors walked together. Your line: eight together. Today a new block begins, with a book.

Some books you read cover to cover. Some you live in. For the next hundred and twenty-one days, this path lives in one: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings of the Buddha. Not every page, but its highlights, in order. A man alone in a forest at night, waiting for fear to arrive. A raft. A saw. A water snake. A murderer who becomes a monk. A man shot with a poisoned arrow who won't let the doctor touch it until he knows who fired it.
screen: `A BOOK TO LIVE IN.` → `A RAFT, A SAW, A WATER SNAKE.` → `THE POISONED ARROW.`

segments.voice: Nikaya means a collection, a group. Majjhima means middle. The discourse basket of the Pali canon holds five nikayas, sorted partly by length: the Long Discourses, the Middle-Length, the Connected, the Numbered, and a collection of shorter books. The middle one holds a hundred and fifty-two discourses, in three sets of fifty, with fifty-two in the last. Mostly the Buddha speaks, but not only. Sariputta teaches. Mahakaccana unpacks a riddle. The nun Dhammadinna answers hard questions. Kings, brahmins, Jain ascetics and wandering philosophers walk through, and a murderer named Angulimala. Some well-known teachings live here: the foundations of mindfulness in MN 10, the raft in MN 22, the noble search in MN 26, the poisoned arrow in MN 63, Angulimala in MN 86. Tradition says these discourses were recited together after the Buddha's death and carried for centuries by memory, by monks who specialized in chanting particular collections, before being written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE. In English, Lord Chalmers' translation, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, appeared in the 1920s; these lessons lean on it and on the Pali, mostly retold. And the book has the feel of a real world. People argue. People misunderstand. Some walk away unconvinced, and the reciters kept those too.
screen: `NIKAYA — A COLLECTION.` · `152 DISCOURSES, THREE FIFTIES.` · `SARIPUTTA, KINGS, A NUN, A MURDERER.` · `CARRIED BY MEMORY, WRITTEN LATER.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE LENGTH.`

segments.voice: Read these titles slowly: the root of all things, all the taints, heirs in the teaching, fear and dread, the simile of the cloth, the simile of the saw, the water snake, the anthill. Let one catch you, without asking why. Then rest with the breath, and let that one title sit beside you.
Majjhima Nikaya. The Middle-Length Sayings: a hundred and fifty-two discourses, our book for the next stretch of the path.
Your line: the middle length. A book to live in, a little at a time. Day four hundred one, and a new block.

402.title: The root of all things
402.hook: the untaught make everything "mine", even nibbana; the monks were not pleased (MN 1)
402.howItsDone: Theravada monastics and scholars often study the Mulapariyaya Sutta as a famously difficult text; many teachers use it to point to the habit of making experience into 'me' and 'mine'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings. Your line: the middle length. Today, page one.

Most of the discourses end the same way: the monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words. It's the canon's standing ovation, again and again. The very first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends differently. The Buddha finishes speaking, and in the edition most translators follow, the text says plainly: the monks did not delight in what he said. First discourse. First page. Not pleased.
screen: `MOST DISCOURSES END DELIGHTED.` → `THE FIRST ONE DOESN'T.` → `NOT PLEASED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mulapariyaya, MN 1. The Buddha walks through everything a person could think of: earth, water, fire, air; beings and gods; the seen, the heard, the sensed, the known; unity and diversity; the all; and, last of all, nibbana. For each, he describes how an untaught person meets it. They perceive earth as earth. Then they conceive: they make earth into me, or put themselves in earth, or set themselves apart from it; they think, earth is mine, and delight in it. Why? Because they haven't fully understood it. The Pali verb is mannati: to conceive, to construe, to build a story with a self in it. And the startling part is the end of the list: even nibbana, the end of grasping, can be conceived and delighted in. Then someone in training, who knows earth directly as earth and is learning not to conceive. And the fully awakened, who don't conceive at all. Why weren't the monks pleased? The discourse doesn't say. A later commentary says these monks had been learned brahmins, proud of their scholarship, and the teaching was aimed at that pride. The Dhammapada makes a similar move, in Max Müller's translation: “These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,” with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth? Being bothered by a teaching sometimes means it found something.
screen: `EARTH, GODS, THE ALL, EVEN NIBBANA.` · `MANNATI — BUILDING A SELF-STORY.` · `KNOWING EARTH AS EARTH.` · `NOT PLEASED, ON PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `NOT PLEASED, YET.`

segments.voice: Let things come: a sound, a feeling in the body, a thought. Watch for the small move that follows, my knee, my plan, my noise, the word mine arriving half a second after the thing itself. You don't have to stop it; just see if you can catch the gap between the sound as sound, and then, mine.
Mannati, to conceive. How an untaught mind turns whatever it meets, even nibbana, into me and mine.
Your line: not pleased, yet. A teaching that bothers you can stay on the table a while. See you tomorrow.

403.title: All the taints
403.hook: seven ways to deal with the taints: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, developing (MN 2)
403.howItsDone: Theravada monastics reflect on the four requisites, robes, food, shelter and medicine, as MN 2 describes, often by reciting a short reflection before using them; the destruction of the taints is a traditional description of awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mannati, building a self-story out of anything, even nibbana. Your line: not pleased, yet.

An old wooden boat has a slow leak. Water seeps in at the seams; you can bail all day and still, by evening, your ankles are wet. One seam needs caulking. Another only leaks when you scrape the rocks, so you steer around them. A third you just live with, and bail. Different leaks, different fixes, and the mistake is using one fix for all of them. The Buddha had a word for what leaks in a mind, and seven ways to deal with it.
screen: `A BOAT WITH A SLOW LEAK.` → `DIFFERENT SEAMS, DIFFERENT FIXES.` → `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: The word is asava, from a root meaning to flow. Translators reach for taints, cankers, outflows. In MN 2, the Sabbasava, the Buddha names three: the taint of sense desire, the taint of being, the craving to exist and keep existing, and the taint of ignorance. Then, instead of one remedy, he gives seven. Some taints are abandoned by seeing: understanding clearly, which comes tomorrow. Some by restraining: guarding the eye and the ear. Some by using: food, clothing, shelter and medicine used for what they're for, not for show or intoxication. Some by enduring: cold and heat, hunger and thirst, hurtful words and pain, borne patiently. Some by avoiding: a wild elephant, a thorny path, a cliff edge, and, right alongside them, bad company. Some by removing: when a thought of greed, ill will or cruelty comes, not putting up with it, but dispelling it. And some by developing: the seven factors of awakening. What makes this practical is that it refuses to use one tool for every job. You don't endure a charging elephant; you step out of its way. You can't avoid hunger forever; some of it you endure. You don't restrain your way out of confusion; you look more clearly. Seven ways, like a ring of keys: the skill is knowing which door you're standing at.
screen: `ASAVA — WHAT FLOWS.` · `THREE TAINTS.` · `SEVEN WAYS, NOT ONE.` · `THE RIGHT KEY FOR THE DOOR.` · then, large: `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that drains you, a habit, a craving, an irritation that keeps coming back, and hold it up to the seven ways, one per breath: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, developing. One of them will fit. Rest with the breath, holding that choice lightly.
Asava. The taints: what flows in the mind and keeps it bound. Sense desire, the craving to be, and ignorance.
Your line: seven ways. The right tool depends on the leak. Day four hundred three.

404.title: Wise attention
404.hook: don't ask "did I exist in the past"; ask "what is dukkha, what ends it" (MN 2)
404.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist schools emphasize wise attention, yoniso manasikara, as the ground of practice; Theravada teachers often present the four noble truths as a way of looking at any experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asava, the taints, and seven ways to meet them. Your line: seven ways. Today, the first way: seeing.

Three in the morning, and the questions start. Who am I, really? What was I before all this? Will any of it matter? What if I've got everything wrong? You can turn those over for hours and get up more tired than you lay down. In an old discourse, the Buddha listed nearly the same questions, almost one for one. Then he said something surprising about them.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `WHO AM I? WHAT WAS I?` → `TIRED BY SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: In MN 2, the first way with the taints is seeing, and seeing depends on how you attend. Unwise attention comes first. A person wonders: Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I? Will I be in the future? What will I be? And now: Am I? Am I not? What am I? Where did this being come from, and where will it go? Then they settle on a view. I have a self. Or, I have no self. Or some other. The Buddha calls all of these a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a fetter of views. Notice that even I have no self is on that list, as a view to get tangled in. He doesn't call the people who ask foolish; he calls these questions unfit for attention. Then wise attention, yoniso manasikara. Manasikara is attention, literally making in the mind. Yoniso comes from yoni, a womb, a source: attention that goes back to where things come from. And it attends to this: this is dukkha; this is its arising; this is its ending; this is the way to its ending. The four noble truths, used as questions. A useful question changes something: where is the suffering in this, what's feeding it, what would ease it? And the text says attention like this cuts three fetters: the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals. Not a small result, for changing what you ask.
screen: `WAS I? AM I? WHAT AM I?` · `A THICKET OF VIEWS.` · `YONISO — BACK TO THE SOURCE.` · `WHAT IS DUKKHA? WHAT ENDS IT?` · then, large: `THE USEFUL QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Find a question that's been circling lately, like why does this always happen to me, and hold it for a breath. Then turn it toward right now: where is the tension in the body, what's feeding it, what would ease it, even a little? No answers needed; just notice whether the new question sits differently.
Wise attention. Yoniso manasikara: attention that goes back to the source, and asks what is suffering and what ends it.
Your line: the useful question. It asks what would ease this, not who you really are. That's day four hundred four.

405.title: Heirs in dhamma
405.hook: be my heirs in the teaching, not in material things (MN 3)
405.howItsDone: Buddhists often cite the Dhammapada line that the gift of the teaching exceeds all gifts, and in some communities giving or sponsoring copies of the teachings, or teaching others, is counted as a gift of dhamma.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wise attention, the question that goes back to the source. Your line: the useful question.

Families can fight over the strangest things after a funeral. Not only the house or the savings. The good china. A watch. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. What people inherit says something about who they were to the person who left. The Buddha, very much alive, once told his monks exactly what he wanted them to inherit from him, and then gave an example to show he meant it.
screen: `THE CHINA, THE WATCH, THE RECIPE CARD.` → `WHAT WILL YOU INHERIT?`

segments.voice: MN 3, the Dhammadayada, opens with one line: monks, be my heirs in the teaching, not my heirs in material things. The word for material things is amisa: flesh, food, the things of the body, and sometimes bait. Then an example. Suppose, the Buddha says, I've finished my meal, and some food is left over, about to be thrown away. Two monks arrive, hungry and weak. I tell them: eat it if you want; otherwise I'll throw it out. The first monk thinks: the Teacher said be heirs in the teaching, not in material things, and this food is a material thing. So he goes without, and spends the night hungry and weak. The second eats, and spends the night comfortably. And the Buddha says the first monk is more to be honored, because it will lead, for a long time, to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, ease in supporting oneself, and energy. It can be an uncomfortable example. The point isn't that food is bad; it opens with the Buddha finishing his own meal. The point is what you reach for when something is offered, and what that habit hands down. Then the Buddha goes into his dwelling, and Sariputta takes over, teaching how a teacher's disciples train in seclusion, or fail to. The Dhammapada puts the value plainly, in Max Müller's translation: “The gift of the law exceeds all gifts.”
screen: `HEIRS IN TEACHING, NOT THINGS.` · `AMISA — FOOD, FLESH, BAIT.` · `TWO HUNGRY MONKS, ONE MEAL.` · `THE GIFT OF THE LAW.` · then, large: `INHERIT THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you hold onto that is only material, a purchase you keep circling, a comfort you reach for out of habit, and imagine setting it down. Then pick up one teaching from these weeks to carry instead: the post holds, your own ground, seven ways, the useful question. Hold that one for the rest of the sit.
Dhamma-dayada, heir in the teaching. The Buddha's wish that his followers inherit his teaching, not his material things.
Your line: inherit the teaching. The best inheritance isn't a thing. Day four hundred five, done.

406.title: Fear and dread
406.hook: alone in the forest at night, he met fear in whatever posture it found him (MN 4)
406.carry: face it where it finds you
406.howItsDone: In Thai and other forest traditions, monks have long practiced in wild and frightening places, including charnel grounds, as a way of meeting fear directly; many teachers also stress keeping precepts as a ground of confidence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhamma-dayada, heirs in the teaching, not in things. Your line: inherit the teaching. Today, the end of the week.

Night in an old Indian forest. No light anywhere but the moon, if that. A man sits alone at a shrine in a grove, the kind of place people avoid after dark. A twig snaps. Leaves rustle. Something moves in the dark. And his heart pounds: here it comes, the fear, the dread. This comes from his own telling, years later. It's the Buddha, before his awakening, describing nights he chose on purpose.
screen: `A SHRINE IN A GROVE AT NIGHT.` → `A TWIG SNAPS.` → `HERE IT COMES.`

segments.voice: MN 4, the Bhayabherava. A brahmin named Janussoni tells the Buddha: forest life must be hard for a monk; the mind of someone without concentration would be swept away. Yes, says the Buddha; I thought so too, before. Then he explains two things. First, conduct. People who go into the forest with harmful actions, speech or ways of living, with greed or ill will, call up fear and dread for themselves. He looked at himself, found his conduct clean, and that gave him great confidence in the wilderness. Second, the fear came anyway. On the special nights of the moon's fortnight, he went to the frightening places: shrines in parks and woods, under great trees. A deer would come by. A peacock would knock down a twig. The wind would stir the leaves. And he'd think: here it comes, the fear and dread. So he made a resolve. Why keep waiting for fear? Why not subdue it in whatever posture it finds me? If it came while he walked, he kept walking until it passed. If he stood, he stood. If he sat, he stayed sitting. If he was lying down, he didn't get up. He never ran to a better position first. And notice what he never says: that he wasn't afraid. He met it where it found him. So the week closes: the path walked whole, the Middle-Length Sayings opened, the root of all things, the taints, wise attention, the heirs, and the forest at night.
screen: `CLEAN CONDUCT, LESS DREAD.` · `A DEER, A PEACOCK, THE WIND.` · `MEET FEAR IN ANY POSTURE.` · `HE NEVER SAYS HE WASN'T AFRAID.` · then, large: `FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Choose a small fear, not the biggest one, an email you haven't opened, a conversation you've been avoiding, and notice where it lands in the body. Then do what the text describes: stay in the posture it finds you, no shifting, no reaching for your phone. Breathe with it until it changes, even a little.
Bhaya-bherava, fear and dread. The terror of lonely places, met by the Buddha in whatever posture it found him.
Your line: face it where it finds you. The fear can come along; you don't have to move. That's the week; see you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're walking alone in a dark grove and fear arrives. what did the Buddha-to-be do, in MN 4?
options: sat down to meditate on it
kept walking until the fear was subdued
ran back toward the village
fork.reveal: he kept walking. he didn't stand, sit or lie down until he'd subdued it. no better position first.

original.note: Pali bhaya-bherava: fear and dread, the terror of wild places; the name of MN 4.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bravery.
what it means: fear met without moving, in whatever posture it arrives, grounded in clean conduct.
what a scholar hears: bhaya is fear, bherava is the dread of fearsome places; the special nights were the fourteenth, fifteenth and eighth of the lunar fortnight.
recall: taints: what flows in the mind

chat.says: How did the Buddha get rid of his fear in the forest?
options: He met it in whatever posture it found him, without moving somewhere safer.
He stopped feeling fear entirely once he started meditating there.
He'd walk back to the village each time and return once he felt calm.
chat.meaning: In MN 4 he resolves to subdue fear in whatever posture it finds him: walking, standing, sitting or lying down. He never says he wasn't afraid.

Bhayabherava.meaning: fear and dread, the fourth discourse of the Majjhima

Janussoni.meaning: a brahmin who says forest life must be hard

brahmin.meaning: a member of ancient India's priestly class
